newsitem.title: FRANCE: Carnage as bomb explodes in Algerian market.
newsitem.headline: Carnage as bomb explodes in Algerian market.

text.p: A bomb ripped through an Algerian market crowded with shoppers on Friday, killing at least three people and wounding 72, Algerian security forces said.
It was the second bomb attack in three weeks on a busy market ahead of Friday Moslem prayers.
Friday's bomb went off at 9.15 a.m. (0815 GMT) in the heart of the market in Kolea, a hill town some 30 km (20 miles) southwest of the capital Algiers.
"The explosion caused the death of three people and wounded 72, including seven in a serious state," the security forces, quoted by the official news agency APS, said.
"Thanks to the rapid intervention of security forces, two other bombs planted in the 'City of 350 Apartments' in Kolea were found and defused," a security force statement said.
It said the toll for the market blast was provisional.

No one claimed responsibility for the bombs but Moslem guerrillas fighting to topple the authorities have been blamed for a series of bomb attacks in which at least 1,400 people have been killed in the past two years.
The market bomb appeared to be part of a campaign by Moslem guerrillas to dispute assertions that security is improving in the North African country.
Attacks on public targets that rapidly become widely known often enable independent newspapers to report the event and give details of casualties despite tight censorship.
Earlier this week, Moslem guerrillas killed at least 34 people in an ambush carried out at a fake security road block.
The security forces gave a death toll of nine for that ambush, but reliable independent newspapers said 34 died, including 20 bus passengers.

"Passengers of a bus were told to get out for identity checks which turned into a nightmare. One by one their throats were coldly slit. Some hostages tried to flee. Some were shot by the terrorists and then finished off and mutilated with knives," said Liberte newspapers.
Diplomats based in Algeria say officials routinely give lower death tolls than reality to echo President Liamine Zeroual's statements that security is improving.
Lack of official action against newspapers that report a higher figure than the official one has long been seen in Algeria as confirmation of the higher toll.
Two Fridays ago a car bomb killed at least seven people and wounded 20 near the market in the town of Boufarik, some 20 km (12 miles) south of Algiers, the security forces reported.

That attack was also carried out just ahead of Friday prayers when markets are crowded with shoppers. The government gave no further details but vowed "the enemies of this nation will be pursued and punished for their horrible acts".
The previous weekend, two bombs exploded in two Algerian towns, killing three people and wounding at least 16.

Algerian security forces and Moslem guerrillas have been locked in conflict since the authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election in which Islamists had taken a commanding lead. About 50,000 people have since been killed.
Zeroual has promised general elections early next year.
Earlier on Friday, APS said officials in charge of security forces and police in 21 Arab countries would meet in Algeria next week to draw on its experience in fighting "terrorism".
